lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: You know the old man — the very ancient one, the rich Eucrates? No sons, but fifty thousand fortune-hunters circling the inheritance.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Yes, the Sicyonian. What about him?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Let him live, Hermes. Add another ninety years to the ones he’s already clocked — more, if you can. But haul down his flatterers one by one: young Charinus, Damon, the whole lot.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: That would seem a bit much.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Not at all. It’s perfectly fair. What have they suffered to earn the right to pray for his death or grab the money when they’re not even related? The worst part is, while they’re wishing for it, they still fawn over him in public. When he’s sick, everyone knows what they’re plotting, but they still promise sacrifices if he pulls through. Their flattery is a work of art. So let him be immortal. Let them go first and choke on their own disappointment.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: They’ll get what’s coming to them — the cheats. He strings them along beautifully, dangles the hope, and despite looking like death warmed over, he’s tougher than men half his age. They’ve already divided the estate in their heads and are living the high life on credit.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Then let him shed his old age like Iolaus and turn young again. And let them drop the wealth they’ve been dreaming of right in the middle of their hopes. Send them down now — dead, and badly.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Consider it done, Pluto. I’ll bring them one by one. Seven, I think.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Drag them down. And he’ll see each one across as a young man again instead of an old one.
